s0201.literal: From this, heroes and outstanding men from the four directions came following heel upon heel; therefore [Qin] could generation after generation be a mighty state, swallow and annihilate the feudal lords, embrace possession of All Under Heaven, and concurrently style itself Emperor—this was because of the assistance of its counsellors.
s0201.idiomatic: As a result, brave and capable men flocked in from every quarter, so that Qin could remain a great power for generations: it devoured the regional states, held the whole realm, and took the imperial title as well—and all of that rested on the strength of its strategists.

s0202.literal: The transforming influence of the Way was not yet pure; [he] collapsed at Sandy Mound.
s0202.idiomatic: Moral transformation had not yet settled when the First Emperor died at Shaqiu.

s0203.literal: Hu Hai rode upon cruelty, employed deceit and misled himself, was unable broadly to sustain the main line of succession and successfully complete the hall-and-rafters legacy, and instead cruelly injured benevolence and righteousness, so poison spread to the black-haired commoners.
s0203.idiomatic: Ershi rode his father's violence, schemed his way to the throne and trapped himself, failed to shore up the legitimate line of rule or finish the edifice his father had raised, and instead trampled human decency until its venom seeped through the common people.

s0204.literal: Therefore Chen Sheng and Wu Guang raised their arms and cried aloud, and All Under Heaven answered in response.
s0204.idiomatic: So Chen Sheng and Wu Guang raised their fists and shouted to the world, and the empire answered from every side.

s0205.literal: Thereupon Zhao Gao rebelled in disorder, Yan Le received his finger[-pointed command], the Second Generation was driven to extremity, and at Wangyi [palace] killed himself.
s0205.idiomatic: Then Zhao Gao turned traitor, Yan Le did his bidding, the Second Emperor was cornered, and cut his own throat at Wangyi.

s0206.literal: Although Ziying was installed, [he] removed the title of emperor and styled himself king; orphaned and imperilled with none to aid [him]; in forty days [he] perished.
s0206.idiomatic: When Ziying finally took charge he demoted himself from emperor to mere king—too isolated and too late—and within forty days the house was gone.

s0207.literal: This was because wicked ministers monopolised commands, pointed at a deer and called it a horse—therefore they hastened Qin's calamity.
s0207.idiomatic: Vicious favourites seized the government, called a deer a horse, and in doing so they hurried Qin to its ruin.

s0208.literal: Qin lost its deer; heroes strove in competition. Xiang Yu grasped it yet lost it; his fault lay in boiling Han Sheng alive, and in Fan Zeng's stratagems going unused.
s0208.idiomatic: When Qin dropped the prize, every warlord lunged for it. Xiang Yu seized the advantage and threw it away—blame the execution of his honest adviser Han Sheng and his refusal to heed Fan Zeng.

s0209.literal: Supposing Yu had already rejected Xiang Bo's perverse counsel, beheaded the Duke of Pei at Hongmen, and established his capital at Xianyang to command the feudal lords—then All Under Heaven would have had no match.
s0209.idiomatic: Had he brushed aside Xiang Bo's bad advice, killed Liu Bang at the Hongmen banquet, and ruled from Xianyang with a finger on every rival, no one in the realm could have stood against him.

s0210.literal: Yet Yu refused Han Sheng's loyal remonstrance, turned his back on Fan Zeng's deep plans, fancied himself already settled in his hegemon-king enterprise, chose Pengcheng as his capital, returned to his home region, and by day draped himself in patterned embroidery—this is merely the sentiment of vulgar sons and daughters, yet Yu gloried in it.
s0210.idiomatic: Instead he spurned Han Sheng's blunt counsel, ignored Fan Zeng's designs, decided the hegemony was already his, lounged back in Pengcheng and his native haunt, flaunting brocaded silks like a suburban parvenu—and he preened over it.

s0211.literal: Therefore within five years he was captured by Han; arriving at this point he still knew no awakening, and proclaimed, 'Heaven destroys me—it is no fault of war'—how very painful!
s0211.idiomatic: Five years later Han had him bound, and even then his only excuse was ‘Heaven has doomed me—not my generalship!’—there is bitterness in hearing it.

s0212.literal: Moreover, shi who turn toward benevolence are like water tending downward or birds fleeing to the wilds; hence it is said, 'Those who for the rivers drive the fish are the otters; those who for the marsh drive the finches are the sparrowhawks; those who for Tang and Wu herd the people are Jie and Zhou.'
s0212.idiomatic: Besides, gentlemen flock to humane rule as water runs downhill or game seeks open ground. The classic line runs: ‘Otters harry fish into the deep pools; goshawks harry sparrows into the brush; tyrants like Jie and Zhou chase the people straight into the arms of founders like Tang and Wu.’

s0213.literal: Closing hook quotation mark. Han Gaozu arose from coarse cloth, grasped a three-foot blade and took All Under Heaven, employed the resources of the six states, had no abdications like those of Tang or Yu—how could it be merely that he relied on the singular schemes of [Zhang] Liang and [Chen] Ping and exhausted the wits of every hero? It was likewise because the Xiang clan drove the people [to him].
s0213.idiomatic: Emperor Gaozu of Han began as a commoner, took up a short sword, and won the realm with the wealth of the six former kingdoms—there was no gracious handover like the legends of Yao and Shun. His victory was not only Zhang Liang's and Chen Ping's cunning or the muscle of every adventurer; the Xiang clan itself herded the population into Liu Bang's camp.

s0214.literal: Sons and grandsons inherited the foundation for more than two hundred years, until it reached Emperor Cheng, who delegated government to his maternal uncles' house and caused power and influence to shift outward.
s0214.idiomatic: His line held the mandate for over two centuries until Emperor Cheng handed the real work to his mother's kin and watched real authority drift beyond the palace.

s0215.literal: Marquis Anchang Zhang Yu was one of Han's Three Dukes and Emperor Cheng's guardian-tutor; the Emperor personally favoured his house, bowed below Zhang Yu's couch, and deeply inquired about Heaven's calamities and human affairs.
s0215.idiomatic: Zhang Yu of Anchang sat among the three highest ministers and had nursed Emperor Cheng as tutor; the sovereign made personal calls on his estate, kowtowed beneath the old man's daybed, and pressed him for guidance on portents and policy.

s0216.literal: Yu ought to have upheld a great minister's integrity, deeply pondered for the altars of soil and grain, offered loyal words and excellent plans, set forth its disasters and worries—then the Wang clan could not have monopolised favour and power, Wang Mang would have lacked a chance to ride momentum and rank, ascend by the cloud-dragon metaphor to the celestial thoroughfares, and cause Han's imperial fortune to snap mid-course.
s0216.idiomatic: A man in his station should have spoken for the dynasty, weighed the fate of the altars in good faith, and laid the dangers plain; if he had, the Wangs could never have hoarded every lever, Wang Mang would never have climbed the dragon's mist into power, and the Han mandate might not have broken halfway.

s0217.literal: Yu was sycophantic and unfaithful, harboured private calculations, merely lowered and raised his head among the Five Marquises, and crudely sought favour and flattery.
s0217.idiomatic: Instead Zhang Yu flattered his way through the Wang circle, trimming his sails between the Five Marquises and angling only for smiles from the throne.

s0218.literal: Therefore Zhu Yun, upholding integrity, demanded the Shangfang [imperial armory] sword for beheading horses, intending to behead Yu, to warn the rest—this can be called loyal.
s0218.idiomatic: So Zhu Yun defied protocol to demand the palace armory's horse-beheading blade, ready to strike Zhang Yu's head off as an example—it was fidelity of the courageous sort.

s0219.literal: Yet Emperor Cheng still did not awake; indeed he judged it railing from below upon those above and court insult to guardian-tutors—as a crime deserving death without pardon—and ordered the censor escort Yun down [to judgement], intending to boil him hurriedly.
s0219.idiomatic: Even then Emperor Cheng would not wake up: Zhu Yun was somehow a criminal for shaming tutor and emperor alike, deserved execution without appeal, so the clerks hurried him toward the boiling cauldron.

s0220.literal: Yun clung to the palace hall and broke the threshold; fortunately he relied on General of the Left Xin Qingji knocking his head until it bled, contending for him with his life.
s0220.idiomatic: Zhu Yun had to clutch the hall balustrade and snap the marble rail before General of the Left Xin Qingji could batter his brow bloody and buy his life with his own safety.

s0221.literal: Had it not been so, then Yun would already have been shattered to pieces.
s0221.idiomatic: Without that intervention he would have been torn apart on the spot.

s0222.literal: Although afterwards [the court] released [him from] the stock and did not repair [the threshold], intending thereby to display the upright minister, truly it may suffice as a warning for later ages—what benefit had it for the reason Han house thereby perished!
s0222.idiomatic: Later they left the broken rail unrepaired to advertise a straight speaker—fine theatre for the chronicles, but it did nothing to cure the illness that would kill Han.

s0223.literal: Yet debaters of the age judge that among disorderly ministers and unfilial sons none without the Way exceeded Mang to such a degree—this too is like saying Zhou [Xin]'s wickedness did not reach such an extreme.
s0223.idiomatic: Later writers treat Wang Mang as the worst traitor imaginable, much as moralists pretend King Zhou's evil was unmatched—both judgments overstate the case.

s0224.literal: The tradition states that Mang at first arose from maternal relatives, bent his demeanour and exerted conduct, thereby to seek reputation; his lineage kin called him filial, friends returned to his benevolence.
s0224.idiomatic: Records say Wang Mang began as an in-law who cosplayed austerity, curried a spotless name until kinsmen praised his filial piety and friends swore to his kindness.

s0225.literal: When it reached his assisting government at the juncture of Emperors Cheng and Ai, he toiled for the state, and in action he was praised and recounted.
s0225.idiomatic: By the Cheng and Ai reigns he looked busy on the state's behalf, and every gesture drew applause from the chroniclers.

s0226.literal: Yet at that time gentlemen who went to the palace gate to submit memorials recommending Mang could not be fully recorded, and among inner and outer ministers none failed to attribute merit and virtue to Mang.
s0226.idiomatic: Memorials praising him stacked up at the palace gate faster than anyone could count, and every courtier, inside or out, sang of his genius and virtue.

s0227.literal: Meeting Han house in mid-decline, the imperial heir three times cut off, while the Grand Empress Dowager enjoyed long years and served as its ritual head—therefore Mang could carry out the abdication edict for the child emperor and wrest his throne.
s0227.idiomatic: Han was already hollow, the succession had failed three times over, and the aged Grand Empress Dowager remained the ritual figurehead—so Mang could stage the script for the boy ruler and walk off with the talisman.

s0228.literal: Formerly Tang's and Wu's rise likewise took by revolt yet preserved by compliance.
s0228.idiomatic: Even Tang and Wu had seized power by force before they secured it through just rule.

s0229.literal: If Mang had deeply pondered Yin and Zhou's arts of taking and preserving, honoured virtue, applied himself to benevolence and righteousness, practised trustworthiness and substance, cast off flourish and falsity, spread kindness over All Under Heaven for eighteen years, so that kindness could move the hundred surnames and righteousness could bind the heroes, with every heart cherishing his virtue and stalwarts employed together—thus, the ancestral temple and altars of soil and grain ought not yet to have perished; though Guangwu might again be gifted with talent, how could great enterprise have been hoped for!
s0229.idiomatic: Suppose Wang Mang had studied how early dynasties won and kept the throne: he might have cultivated genuine benevolence, kept his word, shed the theatrical virtue, and spent eighteen years actually feeding the realm until the people cherished him and bold men rallied. The altars might still stand; even a genius like Guangwu would have had no opening.

s0230.literal: After Mang ascended the throne, he deemed himself assisted by Heaven and man, thought his merit vaster than the Three Kings and his virtue lusher than Tang or Yu, and therefore grew prideful, flaunted his might and deceit, promulgated talismanic prophecies, displayed violence and cruelty, exhausted what's most vicious and evil, so man resented and spirits raged; in winter thunder and lightning startled his ears and eyes, in summer the earth quaked to warn his heart and belly.
s0230.idiomatic: Once enthroned he decided Heaven and humanity were his sponsors, bragged that he outshone the Three Kings and rivalled Yao and Shun, then turned swaggering and cruel, peddled forged omens, and ruled by terror until men and gods alike cursed him—winter lightning slapped his ears, summer tremors nagged at his gut.

s0231.literal: Yet Mang still knew no awakening; he just then again heavily enforced untimely ordinances, extended to the linked-five[-household] punishments, treated the sycophantic as intimate favourites, and executed and exterminated those who loyally remonstrated.
s0231.idiomatic: He still would not learn: he doubled down on senseless edicts, chained neighbours into collective guilt, promoted flatterers, and slaughtered anyone who told the truth.

s0232.literal: From this All Under Heaven seethed with anger, inner and outer alike erupted, the four seas split and crumbled, city walls were not preserved, he died in the hands of a common fellow, and became the laughingstock of the realm—how is it not strange!
s0232.idiomatic: The realm boiled over, revolt flared inside and out, and when the frontiers collapsed he died at a commoner's knife—an empire's joke. How could it be otherwise?

s0233.literal: What from this ensued was not excess in taking, but guarding by a way that was not the Way.
s0233.idiomatic: The failure was not that he had stolen the throne but that he guarded it without rectitude.

s0234.literal: Mang having already slaughtered down to [the people's] flesh, the six directions were roiled like clouds; Liu Shenggong was already enthroned yet could not impose order; Penzi succeeded him yet overturned in defeat; Gongsun Shu again styled himself emperor in Shu-Han.
s0234.idiomatic: When Wang Mang's butcheries had left the populace raw, turmoil rolled through every quarter: Liu Xuan styled himself emperor but never imposed order; Liu Penzi inherited the sham and collapsed; then Gongsun Shu declared another court in the southwest.

s0235.literal: Such several sons, by their nature, are not what one calls answering Heaven and complying with humanity; they merely acted as Guangwu's swept-path men.
s0235.idiomatic: None of those men truly answered Heaven's charge or embodied the people's will; they merely cleared Guangwu's path for him.

s0236.literal: As for All Under Heaven, in general it is likewise All Under Heaven's All Under Heaven—it is not one man's All Under Heaven.
s0236.idiomatic: The realm belongs to everyone who dwells under Heaven, not to a single occupant of the throne.

s0237.literal: 'The hosts of Yin and Shang, their assembly like a forest; arraying at Shepherd Wild, here our noble lord mounts.'
s0237.idiomatic: The ode runs: ‘The Yin-Shang legions gathered thick as timber; arrows flew at Muye—for us the march-lord sparks the charge.’

s0238.literal: Closing hook quotation mark. Again it states: 'The noble ranks obey Zhou—Heaven's Mandate is not constant.'
s0238.idiomatic: Elsewhere it adds: ‘When vassals bow before Zhou's king, Heaven's decree shifts without fixed rule.’

s0239.literal: Closing hook quotation mark. From this speaking it, the ruler is not an ordinary person: possessing virtue then All Under Heaven returns to him, lacking virtue then All Under Heaven rebels against him.
s0239.idiomatic: From those verses it follows that the sovereign cannot be judged as an ordinary man: virtue draws the realm toward him; its absence pushes it away.

s0240.literal: Therefore ancient enlightened kings worried their minds and pondered distant [matters]; constantly it was as facing a river without ford or bank.
s0240.idiomatic: The wisest kings of old wore themselves down with long views, always feeling as though they stood on a riverbank with neither bridge nor opposite shore.

s0241.literal: Thereupon they modelled Heaven and earth, patterned the four seasons, magnified gracious virtue, revered great ministers, drew near loyalty and straightforwardness, and kept distance from sycophants.
s0241.idiomatic: So they took heaven and earth for their pattern and the seasons for their rhythm; they thickened kindness, honoured high ministers, kept honest advisers close and flatterers at arm's length.

s0242.literal: Benevolence and filial piety shone inside the palace walls; extensive transformation harmonised the myriad commoners;
s0242.idiomatic: Filial tenderness lit the women's quarters while his moral influence steeped the myriad households;

s0243.literal: [His] deportment stood straight level as grindstone arrow[-shafts]; trust and righteousness moved humans and spirits.
s0243.idiomatic: his manner stayed straight as polished arrow-shafts on a whetstone, and sincerity moved both subjects and unseen powers.

s0244.literal: Although there existed favour for empress chambers and maternal kin, [he] did not accept their roundabout words;
s0244.idiomatic: Even when imperial in-laws leaned on palace favour, he refused their roundabout pleas;

s0245.literal: although there existed close-attendant favourites of the petty sort, [he] did not heed their placating rhetoric.
s0245.idiomatic: even intimate eunuchs and painted favourites failed when they cooed placations.

s0246.literal: The four gates were solemnly ordered, stood open yet not barred shut, awaited remonstrators without taboo.
s0246.idiomatic: The four gates stayed ceremoniously open—never barred against the man who came to remonstrate.

s0247.literal: Constantly trembling and shivering, not forgetting caution and dread—thereby intending forever to conclude Heaven's stipend yet fearing to become swept-path fare for sage worthies thereafter.
s0247.idiomatic: They shivered awake every night lest they squander Heaven's bounty and someday play stepping-stone to worthier heirs.

s0248.literal: Moreover your servant has heard it said: One who dreads peril is perpetually secure;
s0248.idiomatic: Your subject has also heard that those who dread danger usually stay upright;

s0249.literal: one who worries about perishing endures perpetual survival.
s0249.idiomatic: those who rehearse catastrophe tend to endure.

s0250.literal: If lords possessing the state could be secure yet not forget peril, then root and branches [would flourish] hundred generations, long preserve honoured fortune, fame and standing [would be] limitless with Heaven and earth—is there then worry over becoming swept-path fare for whoever comes!
s0250.idiomatic: Let any ruler clutch safety without forgetting peril, and the dynastic trunk will sprout centuries of shade, honours will hold until sky and soil wear out—and who then needs dread being another founder's prelude?

s0251.literal: The tradition possesses a saying: 'The madcap's speech—an enlightened ruler scrutinises it.'
s0251.idiomatic: The classics insist: ‘Even reckless talk deserves a clearsighted ruler's ear.’

s0252.literal: The second reads: Establishing deed for shi is not alike in conduct on a single model.
s0252.idiomatic: The second strand says: gentlemen build careers along more than one moral road.

s0253.literal: Wu Qi coveted office, [when] his mother died did not return, killed his wife to seek generalship—extremely unfilial.
s0253.idiomatic: Wu Qi chased rank without burying his mother and murdered his wife for a command—monstrously unfilial.

s0254.literal: Yet in Wei he caused Qin people not to dare face east;
s0254.idiomatic: Yet in Wei he froze Qin's armies from turning east;

s0255.literal: in Chu, then the three Jins did not dare plot southward.
s0255.idiomatic: in Chu he kept the three successor states from striking south.

s0256.literal: Zeng Shen and Min Qian were truly filial sons; they could not overnight leave their kin—how could they be willing to emerge body to die, wading into perilous places!
s0256.idiomatic: Zeng Shen and Min Qian were paragons of filial piety who would not leave a parent's side for a single night—hardly the sort to charge into mortal danger abroad.

s0257.literal: Now Great Jin has received what the ordained moment confers—the sage clarity matches Yu [-Shun's reign]—yet Wu people do not submit as ministers, privately attach and style themselves emperor; this likewise is the state's shame.
s0257.idiomatic: Under Great Jin Heaven has delivered its mandate—the court's enlightenment rivals the age of Yu—yet the Wu regime still withholds tribute and enthrones itself, which remains a blot on imperial dignity.

s0258.literal: If Your Majesty truly wishes to summon bear-like warriors and ministers whose hearts know no divided loyalty—such as make might flourish along the Huai shore and awe the barbarous Jing—then rightly you ought to enquire everywhere, broadly gather, widen the road presenting tribute scholars, recommend [men from] crag caves, raise worthy talent, summon by edict them to examination—and employ none who are not eminent.
s0258.idiomatic: If you mean to leash real fighters and steadfast ministers—the kind whose roar freezes the Yangzi marshes—you must cast the net wider: open avenues for recommended scholars, pull talent out of hillside recluses, issue summons and probationary posts, and refuse anyone who lacks distinction.

s0259.literal: Now Tower-Pavilion selections block eyes and ears, the Nine Ranks enquire into men only by asking the impartial rectifier.
s0259.idiomatic: Today Secretariat appointments stumble blind: the nine-grade system reduces every judgment to whatever the local rectifier whispers.

s0260.literal: Therefore those occupying highest rank are, if not ducal marquises' grandsons, then those in power's elder-younger brothers.
s0260.idiomatic: So the top slots go either to sons of old title-holders or to brothers of whoever currently pulls the strings.

s0261.literal: If the two are thus, then how should not the outstanding of brushwood-gate thatched-houses have sunken landwards!
s0261.idiomatic: When blood and connection alone advance, how can brilliant men from drafty hovels avoid sinking unread?

s0262.literal: The third reads: Formerly Tian Zifang maintained old horses, and indigent shi knew where to return—how much more dwelling in All Under Heaven's vast dwelling, standing in All Under Heaven's correct position, walking All Under Heaven's great road!
s0262.idiomatic: The third theme: when Tian Zifang kept his worn-out horses fed, every poor scholar knew where to find shelter—how much more should a Son of Heaven, who lives in the world's broadest house, stands on its central dais, and walks its kingly path, show the same care!

s0263.literal: Formerly enlightened kings and sagely lords none failed to nourish the aged.
s0263.idiomatic: Every sage king of old honoured the elderly.

s0264.literal: The aged multitude, not necessarily all worthy, cannot all be nurtured.
s0264.idiomatic: Gray hair multiplies faster than virtue; you cannot pension every grandfather in the empire.

s0265.literal: Therefore treating as father the three elders manifests filial piety;
s0265.idiomatic: That is why the ritual ‘father service’ toward the trio of elders broadcasts true filial example;

s0266.literal: ritually treating as ancestors the Five Superiors manifests reverence.
s0266.idiomatic: why the ancestral-style honour paid to five senior exemplars broadcasts respect.

s0267.literal: Mengzi stated: 'I extend honoring my elders to honoring others' elders; I extend loving my young to loving others' young.'
s0267.idiomatic: Mencius said: ‘I honour my elders and carry that honour outward; I cherish my children and widen the same tenderness to theirs.’

s0268.literal: Closing hook quotation mark. Now though All Under Heaven is settled, south of Mount Hua there are not herds releasing horses; beneath Peach Grove there are none resting oxes—thus because Wu people still have not bent in submission.
s0268.idiomatic: Though the empire is nominally quiet, nobody is pasturing peace horses south of Huashan or spelling ox teams beneath Taolin—Wu still withholds homage, and martial readiness cannot end.

s0269.literal: As for starving men easy become food, thirsty men easy become drink; All Under Heaven's common folk gaze toward the new governance.
s0269.idiomatic: The famished welcome any bowl; the parched accept any cup—the common people are watching this new reign with hungry hope.

s0270.literal: May Your Majesty ponder Zifang's benevolence, recall the toil of dogs and horses, consider the carriage-canopy requital, issue a humane and gracious edict, and broadly open a system nourishing the aged.
s0270.idiomatic: Reflect on Tian Zifang's compassion, repay the beasts of burden who served the campaigns, remember the ruler who spared an old carriage for its faithful horse, promulgate a generous decree, and widen every old-age stipend.

s0271.literal: The fourth reads: As for laws, commands, rewards, and punishments, nothing is greater than trustworthiness.
s0271.idiomatic: The fourth theme: in law, orders, rewards, and penalties, nothing outweighs keeping faith.

s0272.literal: The ancients had a saying: 'A person yet lacking trustworthiness—one does not know how he may [be employed].
s0272.idiomatic: The proverb runs: ‘A man who cannot keep his word is not worth hiring for anything.’

s0273.literal: Closing hook quotation mark. How much more nourishing people with bounty, employing people with righteousness—yet could one practise these without trustworthiness!
s0273.idiomatic: How much more true when you feed the people with kindness and command them by duty: who will follow a lie?

s0274.literal: Your servant formerly was West Commandery governor, when the province transmitted down the 'Jiwei' imperial edict: 'Qiang and Hu are road-distant—only enlist those happy to go; those unhappy, do not force.'
s0274.idiomatic: When I governed the western commandery a provincial copy of the Jiwei edict arrived: ‘The Qiang and Hu live far off—recruit only willing volunteers; never drag the reluctant.’

s0275.literal: Closing hook quotation mark. Your servant received the edict, then spread grace and recruited broadly, showed them bounty and reliability, obtained persons' names, and memorialised them item by item to General Who Conquers the West.
s0275.idiomatic: I announced that order, opened my purse wide, spelled out stipends honestly, rostered each volunteer, and filed the register with General Who Conquers the West.

s0276.literal: As for Jin people themselves they could be differentiated and selected stalwart ding[-males] by lawful regulation levies;
s0276.idiomatic: Ethnic Jin households could supply conscripts through the ordinary roster;

s0277.literal: as for Qiang and Hu, without gracious intent informing and instructing them, none desired to ford Jincheng and west of the river.
s0277.idiomatic: but the upland tribes would never have crossed toward Jincheng and the corridor west of the Yellow River without coaxing guarantees.

s0278.literal: From-of-old whenever raising armies crossing the river not once were there disturbances; hence Governor Guo Sui persuaded the marshal with methods, profoundly added rewards and urgings, and promised weighty repayment.
s0278.idiomatic: Earlier campaigns across the river had never turned mutinous, so Governor Guo Sui managed the column with skill, heaped praise, and swore a fat reward.

s0279.literal: Therefore those recruited, grateful for profit and bounty, thereupon established merit and effect; merit ranked first.
s0279.idiomatic: The recruits repaid generosity with courage, nailed the mission, and finished top of the merit list.

s0280.literal: Now prefecture governors and overseer-generals have together already received investiture [rewards]; Qiang and Hu stalwarts perhaps [made] kings or marquises—yet do not receive narrative of discussion [for rewards].
s0280.idiomatic: Today every provincial chief has his patent of honour, while the Qiang and Hu companies who actually won the field—some even ennobled as kings or marquises—watch their claims vanish from the deliberations.

s0281.literal: Duke Wen of Jin still was not greedy for Yuan and broke trust; Duke Huan of Qi still did not spare territory and betray the covenant—how much more a sage lord!
s0281.idiomatic: Duke Wen of Jin refused to cheat his way to Yuan, and Duke Huan of Qi refused to betray an ally for turf—surely Our Sage can outdo petty faithlessness.

s0282.literal: The fifth reads: Formerly Zhou and Han arose, planted kin and established virtue; Zhou relied on the five-grade nobility, Han possessed the river-mountain oaths.
s0282.idiomatic: The fifth theme: Zhou and Han both rose by enfeoffing kin and weaving moral obligation—Zhou through its five ranks, Han through the iron pledge carved on the mountain.

s0283.literal: When it reached their decline, the divine regalia was wrested from weighty ministers, the state's fortune shifted to other men.
s0283.idiomatic: At their fall the sacred vessels passed to overmighty servants and the dynasty's luck jumped surnames.

s0284.literal: Therefore what extinguished Zhou was Qin—not the Ji surname;
s0284.idiomatic: Zhou ultimately fell to Qin, not to another branch of Ji;

s0285.literal: what replaced Han was Wei—not the Liu lineage.
s0285.idiomatic: Han yielded to Wei, not to another house of Liu.

s0286.literal: As for today's great state blueprint: causing different surnames to lack parcels of earth and monopoly enfeoffed townsites, causing same surname jointly to occupy cities linked like strings—supposing moreover you command various kings' posterity grandsons therein to revert to mutual annexation—probably it is likewise Chu men losing Fanruo amidst Yunmeng, still not construed as losing their bow.
s0286.idiomatic: Our present design bars outsiders from walled fiefs while stacking linked citadels in princely hands; even if those same princes claw each other apart later on, it is still like the Chu huntsman losing his Fanruo bow at Yunmeng—someone else's gain, barely a scratch on Chu itself.

s0287.literal: As for thereby the divine regalia not shifting to other lineages—then Founding Ancestor's non-shifting shrine, myriad years and trillionfold will not alter its names.
s0287.idiomatic: Keep the celestial symbol from drifting to strangers, and the founder's evergreen shrine retains its honours forever unaltered.

s0288.literal: Great Jin possesses over twenty kings, yet dukes marquises earls viscounts barons numbering over five hundred polities—wishing to declare their states all small?, then Han Ancestor's rise equally lacked even a chi of territory—how much more those possessing states!
s0288.idiomatic: Great Jin divides more than twenty princes among upwards of five hundred titled baronies—were we to sniff that those plots are petty, recall that Emperor Gaozu began without a thumb's breadth of soil, while these lords already hold cities.

s0289.literal: Or shall we say Great Jin age after age is sagely while the feudal lords' descendants are constantly unworthy?—then Fangxun was perspicacious yet had Danzhu; Gusou was foolish and vicious yet surfaced Yu Shun.
s0289.idiomatic: Neither can one pretend every future prince will be worthless while Jin stays perpetually luminous—Yao the glittering sire still fathered Danzhu, yet blind brutish Gusou spawned Shun.

s0290.literal: All Under Heaven has affairs none not stemming from armies; yet groundlessly many planting army roots broadly opens rebellion's origins—your servant thus states the five-grade [system] is not convenient.
s0290.idiomatic: Every crisis begins with armies, yet gratuitously multiplying warlord bases pours fuel on rebellion—so Your Servant urges that the Zhou-style pyramid of five ranks spells trouble.

s0291.literal: Your servant judges one may enact the prior memorial: the kings ought to enlarge their polities and increase their soldiery, entirely dispatch guarding the border fiefs, enable terrain and disposition sufficient to interconnect—then Your Majesty can pillow high yet lie.
s0291.idiomatic: Adopt last year's proposal: widen princely domains and their garrisons, station them firmly on the borders, tighten their fronts into a continuous shield—after that Your Majesty truly can sleep on a piled pillow.

s0292.literal: Your servant judges the feudal lords earls viscounts barons' titles all ought be reformed and altered, causing enfeoffment's system—stipends, salaries, ritual order entirely to match All Under Heaven's various marquises' precedents.
s0292.idiomatic: Strip back the dizzying tide of dukes and barons until their patents, salaries, and court ritual match those of ordinary marquises.

s0293.literal: Your servant has heard that one who shares track with an overturned cart has never been secure; one who shares illness with the dead has never lived; one who shares law with a perished state has never survived.
s0293.idiomatic: Your subject has heard: ride the same ruts as a wrecked chariot and you will not stay upright; share a corpse's symptoms and you will not draw breath; copy a dead empire's statutes and you will not endure.

s0294.literal: How much more the towering lofty Great Jin, presently about to ascend Great Mountain, enact the Liangfu fief[-rite], carve stone documenting merit, suspend display without limit.
s0294.idiomatic: Especially now, when lofty Great Jin is ready to ascend Mount Tai, perform the Liangfu thanksgiving rite, and chisel everlasting boasts into cliff stone.

s0295.literal: Ought distantly mirror former dynasties' rise and ruin, deepen thereby strict guard, enabling those who wield matters and flourish brush necessarily to possess records therein.
s0295.idiomatic: Look deep into former dynasties' rises and collapses and shore up every precaution, so annalists setting brush to parchment will preserve a truthful record.

s0296.literal: Formerly Yi Yin was ashamed that his lord was not Yao or Shun—this is why your servant therefore privately harbours fervent zeal, forgetting himself light base.
s0296.idiomatic: Yi Yin could not abide a mediocre king—that is why this memorial burns in me until I forget my own slight station.

s0297.literal: Zhuo's memorial being submitted, the Emperor perused and marvelled at it, promoted him to General Who Clarifies Might, Weixing governor.
s0297.idiomatic: When Duan Zhuo's essay reached the throne, the emperor read it with wonder and raised him to General Who Clarifies Might and governor of Weixing.

s0299.literal: Yan Zuan, style Xubo, was a man of Anhan in Baxi.
s0299.idiomatic: Yan Zuan, whose courtesy name was Xubo, came from Anhan in Baxi commandery.

s0300.literal: Grandfather Pu served Zhang Lu as Chief Clerk, urged Lu to surrender to Wei, and was invested Marquis of Pingle township.
s0300.idiomatic: His grandfather Yan Pu rose to chief clerk under Zhang Lu, persuaded Lu to capitulate to Wei, and earned the marquisate of Pingle township.
